front: Define elasticity and plasticity with examples.
back: Elasticity: a body tends to regain its original size/shape when deforming forces are removed (steel bar, stretched rubber). Plasticity: the body keeps the deformed shape even after forces are removed (putty, mud — ideal plastics).

front: Define stress and give its unit and dimension.
back: Stress = restoring force per unit area = F/A. Unit N m⁻² (pascal, Pa); dimension [ML⁻¹T⁻²]. It is generated internally, equal and opposite to the applied deforming force.

front: What are the three types of deformation, and which state(s) of matter allow each?
back: 1. Longitudinal (tensile/compressive) — length change, ΔL/L (solids). 2. Shearing — shape change, Δx/L = tanθ (solids only, needs tangential cross-section forces). 3. Hydraulic — volume change, ΔV/V under pressure p (solids, liquids and gases).

front: State Hooke's law and the meaning of the constant.
back: For small deformations stress = k × strain. The constant k is the modulus of elasticity (Young's Y, shear G, or bulk B depending on the deformation). One constant alone does not describe all elastic behaviour.

front: Sketch the stress-strain curve of a typical metal and label its key points.
back: O→A linear (Hooke's law); A→B nonlinear but recoverable; B = yield point (yield strength σ_y, the elastic limit); B→D plastic region — unloading at C leaves a permanent set; D = ultimate tensile strength σ_u; beyond D strain grows under falling stress, fracture at E.

front: What makes a material brittle or ductile on its stress-strain curve?
back: If D (ultimate tensile strength) and E (fracture) are close, the material is brittle; if they are far apart, the material is ductile and deforms considerably before breaking.

front: How do elastomers differ from metals elastically?
back: Elastomers (rubber, aorta tissue) have a very large elastic region, but stress is NOT proportional to strain over most of it — no Hooke's law — and they show no well-defined plastic region.

front: Define Young's modulus and explain what 'most elastic' means.
back: Y = (F/A)/(ΔL/L) = FL/(AΔL). 'Most elastic' means deforms the LEAST for a given load: steel needs 2000 N for a 0.1% elongation of a 0.1 cm² wire while aluminium needs only 690 N, brass 900 N, copper 1100 N — so steel has the largest Y among them and is used in heavy machines.

front: Work Example 8.1 in outline: elongation of a steel rod under 100 kN.
In a two-wire (copper + steel) series elongation problem, why is ΔL_c = 2.5 ΔL_s?
back: Same load and area: ΔL_c/ΔL_s = (Y_s/Y_c)(L_c/L_s) = (2.0/1.1)(2.2/1.6) = 2.5. With the net elongation 0.70 mm: ΔL_c = 5.0×10⁻⁴ m, ΔL_s = 2.0×10⁻⁴ m, giving W = 1.8×10² N (Example 8.2).

front: Define the shear (rigidity) modulus. What is its typical relation to Y?
back: G = (F/A)/(Δx/L) = F/(Aθ); σ_s = Gθ, unit Pa. Generally G ≈ Y/3; G is always less than Y, and shear is possible only in solids (e.g. steel G = 84 GPa vs Y = 200 GPa).

front: Outline Example 8.4: shear displacement of a lead slab.
Define bulk modulus and compressibility.
back: B = −p/(ΔV/V) and compressibility k = 1/B = −(1/Δp)(ΔV/V). B is positive (pressure rise shrinks volume). Order: B_solids >> B_liquids >> B_gases; air's B ≈ 1.0×10⁻⁴ GPa is ~a million times smaller than a solid's.

front: Why must ocean-depth compression problems use g = 10 m s⁻² in Example 8.5?
back: The problem gives g = 10 m s⁻² explicitly. p = hρg = 3000×10³×10 = 3×10⁷ Pa, and ΔV/V = p/B = 1.36×10⁻² = 1.36%. Using the water density 1.03×10³ kg m⁻³ instead of 10³ would change the answer slightly — follow the book's stated data.

front: What is Poisson's ratio and what is its range for typical materials?
back: Ratio of lateral (perpendicular) strain to longitudinal strain = (Δd/d)/(ΔL/L). Within the elastic limit and material-dependent; e.g. steels 0.28–0.30, aluminium alloys ≈ 0.33.

front: Derive the elastic potential energy of a stretched wire.
back: F = YAl/L, dW = F dl = (YAl/L)dl; ∫₀ˡ gives W = YAl²/(2L) = ½Y(strain)²×volume = ½σεV. Energy per unit volume u = ½σε.

front: How is elastic behaviour used to design a crane rope?
back: Require A ≥ Mg/σ_y = (10⁴×9.8)/(300×10⁶) = 3.3×10⁻⁴ m² (radius ≈ 1 cm). A safety factor ~10 dictates a thicker rope; it is braided from many thin wires to stay flexible and strong while remaining easy to manufacture.

front: Why is a beam's depth more important than its breadth in bending?
back: Sag δ = Wl³/(4bd³Y): δ ∝ 1/d³ but only δ ∝ 1/b. Doubling d cuts the sag eightfold, doubling b only halves it. Too deep a bar buckles sideways when the load is off-centre — hence the I-section compromise.

front: Why can a mountain on earth be at most ~10 km high?
back: Shear stress at the base ≈ hρg; set equal to the elastic limit of rock (30×10⁷ Pa). h = 30×10⁷/(3×10³×10) ≈ 10 km — consistent with Everest's 8.8 km peak.

front: Common traps students miss in stress-strain problems.
back: 1. Tension in any cross-section is F, so tensile stress = F/A (not 2F/A). 2. Hooke's law holds only in the linear part. 3. Y and G apply to solids only; B applies to solids, liquids and gases. 4. 'More elastic' = smaller strain for the same load. 5. Stress is NOT a vector.
